Allure
al-lūr'
v.t. (to draw by offering something desirable; used of God wooing back an unfaithful people, and of false teachers baiting the newly escaped)
From Old French aleurrer, to bait a hawk with a lure. The Hebrew in Hosea is pathah, to persuade or entice; the Greek in 2 Peter is deleazo, from delear, a bait — the fisherman's word.

Biblical Definition

The most astonishing use is God's own. After chapters of indictment against an adulterous nation, He says: “Therefore, behold, I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak comfortably unto her” (Hosea 2:14). The word therefore follows a catalogue of her unfaithfulness, and what follows it is not a sentence but a courtship. He takes her back to the wilderness, the place of the first betrothal, and there “I will give her her vineyards from thence, and the valley of Achor for a door of hope” (Hosea 2:15) — Achor being the valley of Achan's judgment, now turned into a doorway. The result is a changed relation: “thou shalt call me Ishi; and shalt call me no more Baali” (Hosea 2:16), husband rather than master. The other use is the counterfeit: false teachers “allure through the lusts of the flesh, through much wantonness, those that were clean escaped from them who live in error” (2 Peter 2:18), and their bait is a promise: “While they promise them liberty, they themselves are the servants of corruption” (2 Peter 2:19). Two lures, and the difference is what each leads to — the wilderness and a door of hope, or liberty that turns out to be bondage.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines allure as to attempt to draw to, to tempt by the offer of some good, real or apparent, and notes the word carries both a good and an evil sense.

expand to see more

ALLURE, v.t. To attempt to draw to; to tempt by the offer of some good, real or apparent.

2. To draw or invite to any thing; to entice.

ALLUREMENT, n. That which allures; any real or apparent good held forth as an inducement.

LURE, n. Something held out to call a hawk; hence, any enticement; that which invites by the prospect of advantage.

ENTICE, v.t. To incite or instigate, by exciting hope or desire.

Key Scripture

Hosea 2:14 — "Therefore, behold, I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak comfortably unto her."

Hosea 2:15 — "And I will give her her vineyards from thence, and the valley of Achor for a door of hope: and she shall sing there, as in the days of her youth, and as in the day when she came up out of the land of Egypt."

2 Peter 2:18 — "For when they speak great swelling words of vanity, they allure through the lusts of the flesh, through much wantonness, those that were clean escaped from them who live in error."

2 Peter 2:19 — "While they promise them liberty, they themselves are the servants of corruption: for of whom a man is overcome, of the same is he brought in bondage."

Modern Corruption

God's wooing of an unfaithful people is sentimentalised into unconditional acceptance, and the counterfeit lure is sold as liberty.

expand to see more

Hosea 2:14 is a favourite verse of preaching that has lost the doctrine of sin, quoted to prove that God simply accepts and never confronts. That reading requires stopping at the word allure and ignoring where He takes her. The wilderness is not a comfortable place; it is the place of stripping, where the vineyards she credited to Baal are gone and she is alone with her Husband. And the valley of Achor became a door of hope only because judgment had fallen there first. God's wooing of His people runs straight through discipline, and the tenderness of this passage is inseparable from the severity of the two chapters before it.

2 Peter 2:19 names the bait modern corruption uses more than any other: they promise them liberty. The promise is always framed as release — from a restrictive upbringing, from a moral standard cast as arbitrary, from a doctrine called harsh. Peter's reply is that the men making the offer are themselves the servants of corruption, and that a man is enslaved by whatever overcomes him. Nothing is more characteristic of the sexual and doctrinal appeals of our moment than the vocabulary of freedom, and nothing is a surer mark of what Peter is describing than a liberty that leaves its converts less able to stop.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew pathah, to entice or persuade — Hosea 2:14, Judges 14:15; Greek deleazo (G1185), to bait — 2 Peter 2:14, 2:18, James 1:14.

expand to see more

Hebrew pathah — to persuade, entice; Hosea 2:14, and used of Delilah enticing Samson in Judges 14:15.

Greek deleazo (G1185) — to catch by bait; 2 Peter 2:14, 2 Peter 2:18, and James 1:14 of a man drawn away by his own lust.

Hebrew Achor — trouble; the valley of Joshua 7, made a door of hope in Hosea 2:15.

Hebrew Ishi and Baali — my husband and my master; Hosea 2:16, the changed name of the relation.

James 1:14 uses the same Greek word of the mechanism: drawn away of his own lust, and enticed.

Usage

"“I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness” — the wooing runs through the stripping."

"“The valley of Achor for a door of hope” — the place of judgment made a doorway."

"“They promise them liberty” — and are themselves the servants of corruption."
